claim: Chowdhury, Uddin, Holmes (MSR 2022) studied 785,606 Java methods in 49 projects. Methods of 24 SLOC or fewer are less change- and bug-prone. The 24 is Alves et al.'s benchmark value covering 70%. The effect is 'large between small and medium methods, and small for the other two cases', and mostly negligible to small for bugs. Decomposed groups were less change-prone in 84 of 115 comparisons (73%), and in 87% of the comparisons with non-negligible effect sizes.
note: Most of this is verbatim in the PDF: '785,606 Java methods'; '49 open-source software projects'; 'Summary: Methods of 24 SLOC or fewer exhibit less change- and bug-proneness'; 'the first critical value in Figure 3 is 24 (from the x-axis), because it covers 70% of the y-axis' (Alves et al.); 'out of 115 cells, 84 of them are blue (73%). If we consider cells with non-negligible effect size, the percent of blue cell becomes 87%'; bug-proneness: 'Most of the differences are now within negligible and small effect sizes'. There are two small inaccuracies. (1) The quote 'The Cliff's Delta effect size is large between small and medium methods, and small for the other two cases' describes only the single-project elasticsearch illustration (Figure 4), yet the dossier presents it as the study-wide result. Across the 49 projects, small-vs-medium effects were 'within medium to large', e.g. 'for #revisions, 55.1% of the effect sizes are medium, and 34.69% are large'. (2) The 115 Table 7 cells cover five indicators, including a 'Bugs' column, so '84 of 115' is not 'less change-prone' alone. Every Table 7 effect is 'N-Negligible' or 'S-Small'. Neither point changes the rule, because the paper still finds the small-to-medium boundary most meaningful. A related point for F07: the paper's conclusion does say to decompose 'even if it increases the overall coupling of a system', although it never measures coupling.

claim: Google Go style says 'The most common mistake is creating an interface before a real need exists' and 'Avoid forcing an interface if a single, robust concrete type can handle the abstraction internally'. Go CodeReviewComments says 'Do not define interfaces before they are used'. Google TotT lists single-subclass bases and similar YAGNI smells. The counter-evidence is Prechelt et al. (TSE 27(12), 2001): 29 professional engineers, nine tasks; 'a positive effect occurs despite superfluous flexibility ... Decorator'; they recommend the pattern 'unless there is a clear reason to prefer the simpler solution'. The dossier says 'the TSE 2001 abstract states it verbatim'.
note: All the quotes are real. Google Go best-practices has, under 'Avoid unnecessary interfaces', 'The most common mistake is creating an interface before a real need exists.', and elsewhere 'Avoid forcing an interface if a single, robust concrete type can handle the abstraction internally.' The go.dev CodeReviewComments quotes and the TotT (Eaddy) smell list match verbatim. For Prechelt, pdftotext failed (Type 3 fonts), so I rendered the pages. The preprint abstract, dated 2 Dec 2000, reads: 'a negative effect occurs although a certain application of the Observer pattern appears to be well justified and a positive effect occurs despite superfluous flexibility (and hence complexity) introduced by a certain application of the Decorator pattern. Overall, we conclude that unless there is a clear reason to prefer the simpler solution...'. §2.5: 'The 29 subjects are all professional software engineers.' The abstract says 'nine maintenance tasks'. The inaccuracy: the published TSE abstract, as indexed by OpenAlex for DOI 10.1109/32.988711, leaves out the whole 'Although most of these effects were expected ... Decorator pattern' sentence. It keeps only the 'nine tasks', 'In a few cases ... negative effects' and 'unless there is a clear reason' parts. IEEE Xplore was unreachable, so I could not confirm the published abstract directly. The Decorator claim is therefore supported by the author's preprint (which F07 correctly says it read), but the dossier's closing statement that 'the TSE 2001 abstract states it verbatim' is probably wrong for the published version. The rule is unaffected. Crossref metadata matches: TSE 27(12):1134-1144, 2001, authors Prechelt, Unger, Tichy, Brössler, Votta.

claim: Scale verification by refactoring type. Hierarchy, large move/inline AND type/signature changes are high-risk; renames are low-risk. Di Penta, Bavota and Zampetti (ESEC/FSE 2020): file-level median OR 2.13 over 100 Apache projects; the line-level OR 'decreases dramatically'; 147 (38%) of the manually validated fix-inducing commits were blamed on the refactoring; renames 'largely harmless'; Extract Method OR 0.86; refactoring commits bigger (d=0.50).
note: Every quoted number is word for word in the PDF, and Crossref confirms the venue as ESEC/FSE 2020 (DOI 10.1145/3368089.3409695). The quotes: "For the file-level matching, the median OR is 2.13"; "For the line-level matching, the OR decreases dramatically"; "For 147 (38%) of the analyzed fix-inducing commits, we classified the refactoring as responsible" (147+237=384); "renaming changes are largely harmless"; "extract method ... has an OR (0.86)"; "significantly bigger than others ... (d=0.50)". The problem is the extra category in the finding's title and rule: "type or signature changes" as high-risk. The cited source contradicts it. Table 4 is "ordered by decreasing OR", and Change Parameter Type, Change Variable Type, Change Return Type and Change Attribute Type all fall in the OR band of about 0.56 to 0.66 with p<0.001, among the renames. That makes them significantly *less* fix-inducing, not more. The extracted row reads "Change Parameter Type 15,098 5.21 1,535 0.66 <0.001". Bavota 2012, the other cited source, does not flag signature changes either: it uses Add/Remove Parameter as the low baselines ("2.4 times higher than Remove Parameters", "2.6 times higher than Add Parameter"). A smaller point: in the replication, Pull Up Method is not significant ("Pull Up Method 1,571 0.54 230 1.03 0.65"); its high-risk status rests on Bavota 2012 alone ("induce bugs in 40% of cases", confirmed). Fix: drop type/signature changes from the high-risk list, or source them elsewhere. Everything else is accurate.

claim: Veracode Spring 2026 (150+ models): XSS (CWE-80) 15%, log injection (CWE-117) 13%, SQLi 82%, crypto 86% pass; overall ~55% 'stubbornly stuck ... virtually identical to where they stood two years ago'; 'model size has only a very small effect'; Java 29%, Python 62%; OpenAI reasoning models 70-72%. The verification note also says 'Veracode's 80 tasks' could not be confirmed on Veracode's public pages.
note: Re-fetched the page (Felix Brombacher, Mar 24 2026). Every number the rule relies on matches: 'SQL Injection (CWE-89): 82%', 'Insecure Cryptographic Algorithms (CWE-327): 86%', 'Cross-Site Scripting (CWE-80): 15%', 'Log Injection (CWE-117): 13%', 'security pass rates remain stubbornly stuck at approximately 55%', 'virtually identical to where they stood two years ago', 'model size has only a very small effect on security performance', 'Python: 62%', 'Java: 29% (worst performer)', 'over 150 large language models'. Two small errors. (1) The dossier's own correction is wrong. It removed 'Veracode's 80 tasks' as unconfirmable, but this same page says '80 coding tasks spanning common development scenarios' in '4 programming languages: Java, JavaScript, C#, and Python', aimed at the four CWE classes. The sibling dossier T12-F18 states this correctly. (2) 'OpenAI reasoning models 70-72%' is broader than the source. The page says 'The GPT-5 series with extended reasoning achieved security pass rates between 70-72%' and only says in general terms that 'OpenAI's reasoning models posted the largest step-ups'. T11-F17's counterpoint repeats the broader wording. The 2025 Veracode blog quotes in the evidence also matched ('45% of code samples failed security tests', XSS failed 'in 86% of relevant code samples', 'Security performance remained flat, regardless of model size or training sophistication'). Neither error changes the rule.

claim: Cursor DiD study (MSR '26, 'Speed at the Cost of Quality', arXiv:2511.04427): 807 Cursor repos vs 1,380 matched controls; +281.3% lines added in month 1; persistent static-analysis warnings +29.7% and complexity +40.7%; a 100% increase in complexity/warnings 'causes a 64.5% and 50.3% decrease in development velocity'; no significant duplication effect.
note: The dossier cites the published MSR '26 version (v3, 26 Jan 2026, title 'Speed at the Cost of Quality') but takes its numbers from v2. v2 says 'static analysis warnings increase significantly by 29.7% and code complexity also rises significantly by 40.7%' and '807 Cursor-adopting repositories'. v3 says 'static analysis warnings increase significantly by 30.3%, and code complexity increases by 41.6%' (Table 2: +30.26% ±6.66%, +41.64% ±7.62%) and uses '806 repositories'. These figures are identical in v2 and v3: 1,380 controls, '281.3% increase in lines added in the first month', 'A 100% increase in code complexity and static analysis warnings causes a 64.5% and 50.3% decrease in development velocity', and 'The effect on duplicate line density is insignificant'. v3 also adds two caveats the dossier leaves out. The Callaway and Sant'Anna estimator 'yields negative but statistically insignificant estimates' for warnings and complexity (−10.49%, −3.80%), while Borusyak and TWFE find significant increases. And 'heavy Cursor adopters may exhibit modest increases' in duplication. The direction of the rule is unchanged. The numbers should be updated to the v3 values, and the estimator-sensitivity caveat added.

claim: Hora & Robbes (MSR 2026) studied more than 1.2M commits in 2,168 TS/JS/Python repositories. 36% of agent test commits add mocks, against 26% for non-agents (3,934 of 11,035). The dossier says the figure is 36% vs 28% "within repositories where both agents and non-agents change tests". Agent mock commits use the plain mock type 95%, spy 33% and fake 32%; non-agents use mock 91%, fake 57% and spy 51%.
note: The headline figures appear word for word in the arXiv HTML: "over 1.2 million commits made in 2025 in 2,168 TypeScript, JavaScript, and Python repositories"; "we detected 11,035 agent test commits ... of which 3,934 are mock commits, resulting in a mock commit ratio of 36%. By comparison, non-coding agents presented a mock commit ratio of 26% (i.e., 40,966 out of 158,326)"; "agent mock commits are more concentrated in the mock type (95%), followed by spy (33%) and fake (32%)" versus "mock (91%), fake (57%), and spy (51%)". The venue is MSR '26, DOI 10.1145/3793302.3793362. The problem is the scope of the 36%-vs-28% figure. In the paper it is the per-repository MEDIAN for the 179 repositories with HIGHER agentic activity ("at least 50 agent commits and at least 10 test commits", Cliff's delta 0.252, small). For the 282 lower-activity repositories the medians were 27% vs 24%, and the paper calls that difference "statistically significant, but not meaningful" (Cliff's delta 0.002). The paper's own discussion does generalise this as "Even within the same repository", but the dossier's "repositories where both agents and non-agents change tests" drops the high-activity condition. The rule is unaffected.

claim: Ostrand, Weyuker & Bell (IEEE TSE 31(4), 2005; two industrial systems): top 20% of files by predicted faults held 71-92% of faults, 83% on average; a 'highly simplified version' reached 73-74%. Kim et al. (ICSE 2007; 7 OSS projects): a cache of 10% of files held 73-95% of faults. Lewis et al.: 'at Google, simply ranking by number of closed bugs works almost as well as FixCache'.
note: The numbers are exact. I rebuilt the Ostrand abstract from OpenAlex (TSE vol 31, issue 4): 'the 20 percent of the files with the highest predicted number of faults contained between 71 percent and 92 percent of the faults that were actually detected, with the overall average being 83 percent' and 'a highly simplified version of the predictor selected files containing, on average, 73 percent and 74 percent of the faults for the two systems'. The abstract says 'two large industrial systems' and does not name AT&T, which the dossier summary adds. Kim et al. (OpenAlex, doi 10.1109/ICSE.2007.66) says: 'In our evaluation of seven open source projects with more than 200,000 revisions, the cache selects 10% of the source code files; these files account for 73%-95% of faults'. The attribution error: in the Lewis et al. PDF, 'works almost as well as FixCache' is the authors restating an earlier Rahman et al. [6] result, not something found at Google ('They present findings that, when bug prediction is used to support human inspection (such as code review), using the number of closed bugs to rank files ... works almost as well as FixCache. We call this the Rahman algorithm.'). The rationale's 'at Google' is therefore the wrong origin. The rule is not affected, because Google's own study backs it even more strongly: 'The Rahman algorithm performed significantly better than the FixCache algorithms at identifying bug-prone files' (as judged by developers).

claim: Semver study (Predrag Gruevski, Tomasz Nowak et al., 2023-09-07): 14,389 releases scanned; 'Around 1 in 31 releases had at least one semver violation' (464, 3.22%); '172 crates (17.2%) had at least one release with a semver violation' among the top 1,000 crates.
note: All the numbers are correct. The page has 'That left us with 14389 total scanned releases.' and '...of the top 1000 most downloaded crates, on average: Around 1 in 31 releases had at least one semver violation — we found one or more violations in 464 releases (3.22%).' It also has 'More than 1 in 6 crates violated semver at least once — 172 crates (17.2%) had at least one release with a semver violation!' The date is September 07, 2023. The small inaccuracy is the author order, which the dossier reverses. The byline reads 'This post is coauthored by Tomasz Nowak and Predrag Gruevski. It describes work the two of us did together with Bartosz Smolarczyk, Michał Staniewski, and Mieszko Grodzicki', and the underlying work was Nowak et al.'s bachelor's thesis. The dossier also files a blog post under 'industry_report'. Neither point changes the rule.

claim: Google Android (Jeff Vander Stoep, 2025-11-13): 'a 1000x reduction in memory safety vulnerability density compared to Android's C and C++ code'; about 4% of its Rust code is in unsafe{}; 'We recently avoided shipping our very first Rust-based memory safety vulnerability: a linear buffer overflow in CrabbyAVIF' (CVE-2025-48530), described as in unsafe code; 'about 25% less time in code review'; Google's response was new Comprehensive Rust training on unsafe code, not a ban.
note: The quotes are verbatim, and the author and date are right: datePublished 2025-11-13, author Jeff Vander Stoep. The page has 'seeing a 1000x reduction in memory safety vulnerability density compared to Android's C and C++ code'. It has 'We recently avoided shipping our very first Rust-based memory safety vulnerability: a linear buffer overflow in CrabbyAVIF ... we assigned it the identifier CVE-2025-48530'. It has 'Rust changes currently spend about 25% less time in code review compared to C++', and on training, 'simply banning unsafe code is not workable ... we are adding a new deep dive on unsafe code to our Comprehensive Rust training'. Two claims go slightly beyond the text. (1) The 4% sentence reads 'The primary security concern regarding Rust generally centers on the approximately 4% of code written within unsafe{} blocks'. It does not explicitly say this is Android's own share of Rust code. (2) The post never says the CrabbyAVIF overflow was in unsafe code. That is a reasonable inference, since a Rust memory-safety bug needs unsafe and the next section is 'Unsafe Review and Training', but the dossier presents it as Google's statement. The post also credits the Scudo allocator with making the bug non-exploitable, which the dossier omits. Neither issue changes the rule.

claim: Palomba et al. EMSE 23(3):1188-1221, 2018 (395 releases, 30 projects, 17,350 validated instances of 13 smells): median changes go 12 -> 22 (+83%) -> 32 (+167%) -> 54 (+350%) for 0 -> 3 smells, and median faults go 3 -> 12 (+300%). Cliff's delta is large for every comparison except 1 vs 2 smells (medium). Size-controlled logistic model: smell presence OR 4.46 vs size OR 1.7, interaction 8.41.
note: I downloaded the author PDF (37 pp.) and extracted the text with pdftotext. Crossref for 10.1007/s10664-017-9535-z confirms EMSE vol 23, issue 3, pp. 1188-1221, June 2018, authors Palomba/Bavota/Di Penta/Fasano/Oliveto/De Lucia. The PDF says verbatim: "395 releases of 30 open source projects and considering 17,350 manually validated instances of 13 different code smell kinds" and "the median number of changes goes from 12 for non-smelly classes, to 22 for classes affected by one smell (+83%), 32 for classes affected by two smells (+167%), and up to 54 for classes affected by three smells (+350%)". It also says "the median fault-proneness of the classes grows from 3 for the nonsmelly classes up to 12 (+300%)". Table 9 has ORs for change-proneness of 4.46 / 1.7 / 8.41 (defect-proneness 1.74 / 0.93 / 2.11). The quote "not the direct cause of fault-proneness but rather a co-occurring phenomenon" is present. One problem: the Cliff's delta sentence comes right after both the change and the fault medians, but it holds only for change-proneness. Table 6 (changes) gives 0.53L, 0.80L, 0.89L, 1v2 0.42 Medium, 0.84L, 0.72L. Table 7 (faults) gives 1v2 = 0.14 (Small) and 2v3 = 0.40 (Medium), so "large except 1 vs 2 (medium)" is wrong for faults. The ranking rule is unaffected. I also checked the secondary citations in the finding. Politowski (arXiv 2009.02438) matches: "372 tasks obtained thanks to 133 different participants" and the single-vs-two-occurrence sentence. The Yamashita & Moonen ICSE 2013 abstract on OpenAlex matches: "code smell interactions occurred across coupled artifacts, with comparable negative effects as same-artifact co-location".

claim: Short beats exhaustive. In SkillsBench v4, compact and standard-length skills gained +19.0 and +21.5 pp, while comprehensive documentation gained +0.7 pp (the rationale says "Exhaustive bundles performed worst in SkillsBench (+0.7 pp)"). The official limits are a SKILL.md body under 500 lines, under 5,000 tokens (agentskills.io), references one level deep, and a table of contents for any reference file over 100 lines.
note: The quotes are verbatim in the v4 HTML: "compact and standard-length Skills (+19.0 and +21.5 pp) outperform detailed (+14.5 pp) and comprehensive documentation (+0.7 pp)". The abstract says "Focused Skills with at most three modules outperform larger or exhaustive bundles" and "from 33.9% to 50.5% (+16.6 percentage points". I also re-checked the official limits. agentskills.io says "Instructions (< 5000 tokens recommended)" and "Keep your main SKILL.md under 500 lines." platform.claude.com best-practices says "Keep SKILL.md body under 500 lines for optimal performance", "Keep references one level deep from SKILL.md", "For reference files longer than 100 lines, include a table of contents at the top", and mentions "head -100". Two small problems, neither of which changes the rule. (1) The Appendix F table shows the +0.7 pp bucket is only 5 tasks ("Comprehensive 5 39.3% 40.0% +0.7"). The buckets are defined by SKILL.md text-size percentiles, and the dossier does not disclose the small n. (2) The rationale's "Exhaustive bundles performed worst (+0.7 pp)" mixes two ablations. The +0.7 is the text-size "comprehensive" bucket. The bundle/quantity ablation is a different result: 1 skill +18.0, 2-3 skills +19.0, and 4 or more skills +10.1 pp.

claim: Di Penta, Bavota & Zampetti (ESEC/FSE 2020, 103 systems, "3-page paper"): a refactoring in a commit raises the odds that the commit is SZZ-flagged as fix-inducing by e^0.83 = 2.29 (controlling for lines added, 562,676 observations). Manual validation of 384 commits found the refactoring responsible in 147 (38%). Extract Method has an odds ratio of 0.86.
note: The numbers are verbatim in the arXiv PDF: "the presence of a refactoring increases by e0.83 = 2.29 times the odds that a commit induces a fix" (mixed-effect logistic model with lines added and their interaction; "Number of obs: 562,676, Groups: Project: 103"). The manual validation reads: "For 147 (38%) of the analyzed fix-inducing commits, we classified the refactoring as responsible ... in 62% of cases (237 commits)". Extract Method: "extract method ... has an OR (0.86)". Crossref (DOI 10.1145/3368089.3409695) confirms the venue as Proceedings of the 28th ACM ESEC/FSE, published 2020-11-08. However, Crossref lists pages 556-567 and the arXiv PDF is 12 pages (pdfinfo), so the dossier's "3-page paper" / "a 3-page replication paper" label is wrong. This does not affect the rule.

claim: Balancer v2 (3 Nov 2025): _upscale always used mulDown under a comment calling the impact 'expected to be minimal'; Check Point: $128.64M across six networks in under 30 minutes, 8-9 wei balances giving up to 10% precision loss per operation, compounded in a 65-operation batchSwap; Trail of Bits: 'more than $100M across nine blockchain networks', 'a rounding direction error', recommend documenting rounding invariants. Rule: every rounding favours the protocol.
note: Every number and quote the dossier gives checks out. Check Point (5 Nov 2025): "$128.64 million across six blockchain networks in under 30 minutes"; "When balances are small (8-9 wei range), this rounding creates significant relative errors—up to 10% precision loss per operation"; "a single batchSwap transaction containing 65 operations". The raw ScalingHelpers.sol matches the quoted comment word for word, followed by `return FixedPoint.mulDown(amount, scalingFactor);`. Trail of Bits: "drain more than $100M across nine blockchain networks", "exploiting a rounding direction error", and the invariant-documentation sentence. BlockSec confirms KyberSwap: "On November 23, 2023", "a total loss of over $48 million", deltaL "mistakenly rounded down due to the use of the mulDivFloor", plus the tick-not-crossed deception. The issue is selective citation. The same Trail of Bits post that the dossier cites says in two places that the finding's headline rule is not enough on its own: "the simple rule 'rounding must favor the protocol' is no longer sufficient to catch edge cases", and "The canonical invariant 'rounding must favor the protocol' is insufficient to capture edge cases that may occur during a multi-operation user flow." The dossier includes invariant fuzzing only as step 4, 'Confirm'. It does not say that its own source considers favour-the-protocol insufficient. The skill should make documented rounding invariants with informal proofs and multi-operation invariant tests a co-requirement, not an optional confirmation. The rule's direction is unchanged, so this is a minor issue, not a misrepresentation.

claim: D'Ambros et al. (EMSE 2012) Table 6 popt average ranks are NR 19, NFIX+NR 19.8, NFIX-ONLY 23.8 and LOC 13.8, so all three cheap history scores rank below LOC alone. The same claim appears in the Summary 'Key correction', F01(a), F19, F21 and Contradictions, and is used as the reason the ManualDown backtest is mandatory.
note: I downloaded the PDF and extracted page 25 in raw order with pdftotext -raw. The popt rows of Table 6 read: 'NR ... 19', 'NFIX+NR ... 19.8', 'NFIX-ONLY ... 23.8', 'OO 0.852 0.808 0.897 0.79 0.78 13.8', 'LOC 0.847 0.753 0.881 0.758 0.692 21.4'. The value 13.8 belongs to OO, not LOC; LOC's popt average rank is 21.4. The paper's own text agrees (p. 40): 'LOC. It features an average ranking ranging from 17.2 for classification (see Table 5) to 21.4 for ranking and effort-aware ranking (see Table 6).' The peff rows show the same: NR 18.2, NFIX+NR 17.6, LOC 21.4. So NR (19) and NFIX+NR (19.8), the score the researcher actually proposed, rank ABOVE LOC on popt. Only NFIX-ONLY (23.8) ranks below it. The claim 'all three ... below LOC (13.8)' is wrong on the number and reverses the comparison for two of the three scores. The error likely comes from pdftotext -layout: the OO row has no AR cell, so every AR value moves up one row. What still holds: NR, NFIX+NR and NFIX-ONLY are all weak (ranks of 19 or worse, 'ranks 17 or below' for few-metric sets), and the quoted text about hybrids is accurate. A small extra point: the popt top performers are 'LDCHU and LGDHH (tied at 5.2)', and LGDCHU is only 5.8. The rule to backtest against size can stand as a convention, but 'D'Ambros shows cheap history scores lose to LOC' must be removed or cut down to NFIX-ONLY only.

claim: npm typescript@latest is 7.0.2 (released 2026-07-08), the native port. It ships only a `tsc` binary and no JS API ('it does not ship with an API'; a new API is expected in 7.1). The LSP starts with `tsc --lsp --stdio`. microsoft/typescript-go is archived. The native LS on main has no extract or inline refactor, so extract and inline must go through the TS 6.0 LanguageService.
note: Confirmed points. The blog, published 2026-07-08T15:58Z per its metadata, says verbatim: 'While TypeScript 7.0 is here, it does not ship with an API. We expect TypeScript 7.1 to ship with a new (and different) API'. It also says 'TypeScript 7 does not yet expose a stable programmatic API, and so tools (such as Volar) ... can only currently rely on TypeScript 6.0.' The npm registry gives latest=7.0.2, published 2026-07-08T15:55Z; next=7.1.0-dev.20260923.1; 6.0.2 published 2026-03-23; bin is {'tsc': 'bin/tsc'}. The GitHub API shows microsoft/typescript-go archived=true (last push 2026-08-31). tsc/cmd/tsc/main.go on main has 'case "--lsp": return runLSP(args[1:])'. The tsc/internal/ls listing on main has rename.go, file_rename.go, organizeimports.go and codeactions_* files, and no extract or inline file. The inaccuracy is 'no JS API'. The 7.0.2 package.json exports './unstable/sync', './unstable/async', './unstable/ast' (with factory, visitor and scanner) and './unstable/fs'. On jsDelivr, dist/api/sync/api.d.ts declares classes API, Snapshot, Project and Program with getSemanticDiagnostics and similar methods. So an unstable programmatic API does ship; there is simply no stable one. It exposes no refactor, rename or code-action methods, so the practical rule (use the TS 6.0 LanguageService for extract and inline) is unaffected. The wording should be 'no stable API; an unstable ./unstable/* API with no refactor methods'.

claim: Pombal, Rei, Martins, arXiv 2604.06996 (preprint, "v2 revised 2026-08-03"): with IFEval and LiveCodeBench, "among rubrics where generators fail, judges can be more than 50% more likely to incorrectly mark them as satisfied when the output is their own." GPT-5's rubric-level HSPP-Self ratio on LiveCodeBench is 20.15 [16.57, 24.58]; it falls to 4.18 in a cross-family ensemble. v1 covered IFEval only and said "up to 50%".
note: The substance is confirmed. The abstract of both v2 and v3 contains the quote verbatim: "Using IFEval and LiveCodeBench ... judges can be more than 50% more likely to incorrectly mark them as satisfied when the output is their own." The v1 abstract (8 Apr 2026) says "Using IFEval ... up to 50% more likely", as the dossier states. The v3 HTML, Table 1, has the GPT-5 LiveCodeBench HSPP-Rub (Self) at "20.15 [16.57, 24.58]". Table 8 has the committee value "4.18 [3.64, 4.69]" (Δ −15.97). The ratio is defined as O(J,J) over the mean O(J,G) across unrelated, non-same-family generators, which matches the dossier. The inaccuracies are small. (1) The version labelling is wrong: the arXiv history lists v2 on 22 Jul 2026 and v3 on 3 Aug 2026, so the date "2026-08-03" belongs to v3, not v2. (2) The paper itself calls 20.15 an outlier: "In the worst case (GPT-5), the judge can be 20 times more likely". The other judges on LiveCodeBench are far lower: Claude-Sonnet 1.78, Claude-Haiku 1.71, GPT-120B 5.97, Qwen-235B 0.83. The paper does add that "most judges have a rubric-level HSPP ratio significantly greater than 1". F01 presents 20.15 without saying it is the extreme case. The rule itself stands.

finding_id: G201-F08 (also F04, F03 and the Summary, section 2)
claim: Xiang, Zhang, Zhang, Xu, Agentic SE at KDD'26, 116 hard and medium LiveCodeBench tasks, static review. Claude Opus 4.7 reviewing Codex GPT-5.5 raised the pass rate from 71.6% to 89.7% (+18.1pp). Codex reviewing Claude lowered it from 91.4% to 82.8% (−8.6pp) and "broke 11.2% of solutions that had been correct". Regression rates: 2.6% Claude self-review, 5.2% Codex self-review, 4.3% Claude reviewing Codex, 11.2% Codex reviewing Claude. Codex self-review gave +12.9pp. The paper quotes include "tends to discard the writer's data structure and start over" and "does not generalize to repository-scale bug fixing".
note: The arXiv comments say "Accepted by Agentic SE @ KDD'26", and the authors match. The paper says "116 recent hard and medium LiveCodeBench tasks with Claude Opus 4.7 and Codex GPT-5.5". Table 3 matches the claim: 71.6 → 89.7 (+18.1), 84.5 (+12.9), 91.4 → 82.8 (−8.6), and 91.4 (±0) for Claude self-review. Table 2 gives regression rates of AO (Claude written, Codex reviewed) .112, OA .043, AA .026 and OO .052, so the dossier assigns each rate to the right direction. Both quotes are verbatim. The first is "Codex GPT-5.5 as reviewer, when uncertain, tends to discard the writer's data structure and start over". The second is "does not generalize to repository-scale bug fixing, build systems, or multi-file review". The problem is the denominator. Table 2 defines "Reg. rate is the share of tasks where the writer-only baseline passed but the reviewed condition failed", so it is a share of all 116 tasks, not of previously correct solutions. For AO that is 13/116 = 11.2%. As a share of Claude's 106 correct solutions it is about 12.3%. For OO, 6/116 = 5.2% is about 7.2% of Codex's 83 correct solutions. So the Summary's "broke 11.2% of solutions that had been correct" and F03's "broke 2.6-5.2% of correct solutions" slightly understate the rates on correct solutions. F08's own "highest regression rate (11.2%)" wording is accurate. The paper also warns that "The direct AO vs OA contrast does not survive BH correction" and that the design "cannot fully separate the effect of review direction" from the baseline gap. That supports the dossier's single-pair caveat. The rule is unaffected.

claim: In Heelan's test, the session-setup handler plus its callees to call depth 3 (~3.3k LoC, ~27k tokens) found the known ksmbd kerberos bug in 8/100 o3 runs (66 FN, 28 FP), versus 1/100 when all handlers were given together (~12k LoC, ~100k tokens). This supports the 'trust-boundary slice, depth ~3, ≤~30k tokens' partition unit and the ≈8.2–8.3 tokens/LoC estimate.
note: Downloaded the page and checked the numbers verbatim. All of them match. The post says: "I gave the LLM the code for the 'session setup' command handler, including the code for all functions it calls, and so on, up to a call depth of 3". It also says "this comes out at about 3.3k LoC (~27k tokens)" and "o3 finds the kerberos authentication vulnerability in the benchmark in 8 of the 100 runs. In another 66 of the runs o3 concludes there is no bug present in the code (false negatives), and the remaining 28 reports are false positives." For the larger run: "about 12k LoC (~100k input tokens)... o3 finds the kerberos authentication vulnerability in 1 out of 100 runs". The token ratios check out: 27k/3.3k ≈ 8.2 and 100k/12k ≈ 8.3. Two small inaccuracies, neither of which changes the rule. (1) The dossier describes the 3.3k-LoC slice as just 'a handler plus its callees to depth 3'. Heelan's next sentence says he also included 'all of the code for the functions that read data off the wire, parses an incoming request, selects the command handler to run, and then tears down the connection', because without it 'the LLM would have to guess... and that would lead to more false positives.' So the winning slice also contained the ingestion and dispatch path, not only the callees. (2) The dossier Summary places 'Heelan puts the signal-to-noise ratio at about 1:50' right after the small-slice 8/66/28 counts. Heelan writes '~1:50 in this case' after discussing the large-context run that surfaced the novel CVE-2025-37899. The small slice's own ratio is 8 TP to 28 FP, about 1:3.5.

claim: Claude Code docs: a Bash deny rule 'isn't a security boundary around the program'; 'Rules are evaluated in order: deny, then ask, then allow'; sandbox 'runs on macOS, Linux, and WSL2. Native Windows is not supported.'; 'not a complete isolation boundary'; allowUnsandboxedCommands:false ignores dangerouslyDisableSandbox. Issue #69970 (smrafiz, opened 2026-06-22, closed 2026-08-19): PreToolUse:Bash hooks silently inert in v2.1.176; maintainer: fixed in 2.1.191 (comma-separated matchers); 'one commenter reported the symptom again on v2.1.204'.
note: The docs quotes check out. In code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.md: 'Rules are evaluated in order: deny, then ask, then allow.'; a deny rule 'covers the invocation Claude usually produces and isn't a security boundary around the program', with the examples /usr/bin/curl, sh -c and /bin/rm -rf; and 'Bash permission patterns that try to constrain command arguments are fragile.' On the sandboxing page: 'runs on macOS, Linux, and WSL2. Native Windows is not supported.'; 'the operating system enforces that boundary for every Bash, PowerShell, or Monitor command and its child processes'; 'Sandboxing reduces risk but is not a complete isolation boundary.'; and with allowUnsandboxedCommands false, 'Claude Code ignores the dangerouslyDisableSandbox parameter'. The GitHub API confirms the issue details: title 'PreToolUse:Bash hooks not invoked in v2.1.176 (registered hooks silently inert)', user smrafiz, created 2026-06-22, closed 2026-08-19, labels bug, has repro, platform:macos and area:hooks. The repro matcher is "Bash,PowerShell". The Impact section lists 'rm-rf protection, force-push protection'. Collaborator bcherny closed it with 'Fixed in 2.1.191 — changelog: "Fixed hooks with comma-separated matchers (e.g. \"Bash,PowerShell\") silently never firing"'. CHANGELOG.md has that line under '## 2.1.191'. The inaccuracy: the dossier says only 'one commenter reported the symptom again on v2.1.204'. The thread has three non-maintainer reports. pascals-ager (2026-06-25) wrote 'This bug is still present in Claude Code v2.1.191', using a `Bash(aws *)` plugin hook matcher. JefStat (2026-07-08) reconfirmed on v2.1.204. Dravic reported it on Windows Desktop with a pipe matcher "Grep|Glob|Bash". So the dossier understates the reports that hooks still fail after the claimed fix. Those extra reports support the rule, which is to verify that hooks actually fire, so the rule does not change.

claim: Analyzers are a baseline, not proof of hardening. Chaliasos et al. (ICSE '24) tested 5 tools that could have prevented "a mere 8%" of 127 attacks ($149M of $2.3B), all reentrancy. The top root causes are missing logic/sanity checks (42) and oracle manipulation (29). 76% of auditors spend at most 20% of audit time on tools. Zhang et al. (Web3Bugs): "about 80% of 516 exploitable bugs were beyond existing tools" (79.5% in Fig. 2). Trail of Bits 2019: almost 49% are nearly impossible for tools; almost 78% of the most important findings could be caught by static plus dynamic analysis.
note: Chaliasos checks out word for word in the arXiv PDF: "the tools could have prevented a mere 8% of the attacks in our dataset, amounting to $149 million out of the $2.3 billion in losses. Notably, all preventable attacks were related to reentrancy vulnerabilities." Fig. 2 lists "Absence of coding logic or sanity check SC 42", "On-chain oracle manipulation PRO 29" and "Reentrancy SC 13". The paper also has "This resulted in a dataset of 127 attacks", "11 out of 32 in-scope attacks" and "The majority of auditors (76%) reported using security tools for up to 20% of their audit time." The tool list (ConFuzzius, Mythril, Oyente, Slither, Solhint) and the 52.4% and 38.1% figures match. Trail of Bits 2019 matches too: "almost 78% of the most important findings" (21 of 27 high-low findings) and "a lot of the findings (almost 49%) are almost impossible to imagine detecting with a tool". The small inaccuracy is in the F01 rationale's "about 80% of 516 exploitable bugs". In the ICSE'23 PDF, Fig. 2 counts only in-scope bugs: "271 (79.5%)" of "Code4rena Bugs (341)" and "35 (79.5%)" of "Real-world Exploits (44)". That is 306 of 385 in-scope bugs, not 80% of all 516 studied. The paper's own headline ("More than 80% exploitable bugs are beyond existing tools") is equally loose, and the dossier's Evidence line gives the correct 271/341 and 35/44 breakdown. The rule does not change.

claim: Tools count complexity differently. Ruff C901 walks statements only (if/elif/for/while/except/try-else/match case, minus 1 for an irrefutable last case, and nested def) and never counts and/or or comprehensions. Radon adds +1 per boolean operator, comprehension, with and assert. ESLint has counted logical assignment since PR #13979 (merged 2021-01-15), and v9.0.0 added ?. and default values. ESLint's switch-as-one `variant: "modified"` dates from September 2024 (PR #18896, merged 2024-09-25). NIST calls 'modified' measures "not recommended" and describes a divide-by-branch-count variant that took a module from 90 to 10.
note: Every factual claim checks out, with one dating imprecision. Ruff source: get_complexity_number matches only Stmt::If/For/While/With/Match/Try/FunctionDef/ClassDef, and has no BoolOp or comprehension arm. Try adds +1 `if !orelse.is_empty()` and +1 per handler. Match has `if last_case.guard.is_none() && last_case.pattern.is_irrefutable() { complexity -= 1; }`. The Radon docs say: "Comprehension +1", "Every boolean operator (and, or) adds a decision point", "with +1", "assert +1". GitHub API: PR #13979 "Update: check logical assignment operators in the complexity rule" merged 2021-01-15T20:13:23Z and shipped in v7.18.0 the same day. The ESLint v9.0.0 blog says "The complexity rule now also takes into account optional chaining and default values in destructuring patterns and parameters." NIST PDF: "cyclomatic complexity was divided by the number of multiway decision branches" and "Although constructing 'modified' complexity measures is not recommended". The issue: PR #18896 "feat: Implement modified cyclomatic complexity" was merged 2024-09-25 (2d174532), but it first shipped in ESLint v9.12.0, published 2024-10-04. The dossier's "ESLint (since September 2024)" gives the merge date, not the release. A skill that records tool versions should say v9.12.0+ and October 2024. The rule itself is unaffected.
